title: Why Willowmere Forgot Its Name
text: The village beside Pale Lake was called Lutaomen for four hundred years — 'the Reed-Gate Hamlet' — after the reed-lined path south of the square. Then, in a single winter, a sword-feud between two passing sects fell into the village; three houses burned, twenty-one names were not written down in time, and the reed-path was walked over so often by men in armour that the reeds themselves died. When the next spring came, the survivors planted willows where the reeds had been. The old name was spoken of only in the graveyard, and eventually not there either. Willowmere is the name the living chose; Lutaomen is the name the graveyard still answers to, if you have the wrong sort of ear.

title: The Drowning of the Willow
text: She was a bride from the valley above, given in marriage to the elder son of a Lutaomen headman. On the night before the wedding she walked to the shore to rinse her comb, and the water rose — not with a storm, not with a moon-tide, but by the breath of something in the lake-bed that did not approve of the match. The willow on the shore woke, reached for her with its roots, and pulled her under, perhaps to save her and perhaps to keep her. Four days later the willow itself was half-drowned; the shore had retreated. The groom hanged himself in the bamboo. The match, the willow, and the girl are all still there. The villagers leave offerings. The lake does not return them.

title: The Tune with the Last Note Different
text:
The bamboo sings a tune of seven notes —
it has sung them since any mortal could listen.
But if you hear it once in your life
with the last note different,
that is the bird that was paid to warn you.
Lady Moonbell, the children call her,
and whoever you are, and whatever you became,
go gently — she has already bent the tune
that would have warned you too late.

title: Tea-Mother Weiyu's Ledger
text: Weiyu has kept the accounts of the Willow-and-Moon for thirty-nine years. The ledger has very little to do with money. One page per customer, one column per visit; beside every visit, a single character, in her neat village hand — *zhuo* (turbid), *qing* (clear), *ku* (bitter), *xiao* (whistling), and two she coined herself and will not explain. When a customer dies, Weiyu writes their last cup in red ink and turns the page. Half the pages of the ledger are red; the other half are waiting.
